<reason>Both sides were strong and disciplined, but B built the cleaner path. A's best move was the dilemma in R1: either PRO's tools spare legal planters (abandoning the "even if") or they cut income and need justification. B met this head-on in R2, honestly naming the losers (undeveloped forest concessions, some frontier smallholders), giving a principled rule (harm-stopping never waits on guaranteed compensation), and turning the trap back on CON: A's own prescription of enforcement, titling, and mandated intensification also imposes uncompensated losses A refuses to name. A never squarely answered that, nor B's closing point that enforcement is backward-looking and cannot prevent lawful clearing at the moment a license is signed — the forward-looking route to permanent loss. A's status-quo compensation answer for haze victims ("damages from burners") was thin against B's unanswered "zero for burned lungs" charge, and A never touched the EU deforestation-rule point undercutting the export-growth harm. A's "unpaid childhood is irreversible" line and the closing "even if" indictment landed real hits, but A's R1 was clipped for exceeding the limit (an execution cost) and its closing left B's prevention-vs-enforcement gap standing. B's debt/deletion frame organized the whole debate and survived every challenge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2, A1: under direct pressure from A's Q1, B embraced the "even if," named exactly whose income falls, then exposed that CON's own tools forbid someone's expansion too — "they simply refuse to name their losers" — converting A's strongest dilemma into a burden A never discharged.</best_rebuttal>
